questions.text: I find it puzzling when people say one thing but apparently mean another.
I naturally gravitate toward being the person who introduces people and assigns them roles.
I rarely feel the kind of emotional urgency that demands immediate action.
I tend to frame career conversations around my own aspirations and what I need to get there.
I routinely research and pursue opportunities that specifically strengthen my resume or portfolio.
I often end up as the reliable supporter in group projects.
Other people's pain seldom feels like something that requires a response from me.
I sense when an invitation was extended to one person but worded to include the group so it would not seem exclusive.
Hearing about a crisis affecting others seldom leaves me wanting anything to change for them.
I notice when someone glances at the clock or door during a conversation, signaling they have mentally left.
I let the scope of a task reveal itself as I work rather than defining it upfront.
I notice that I don't carry the physical tension patterns that many people associate with stress.
When something wonderful happens, my elation is so strong it can feel almost manic.
When a report describes people's suffering in impersonal terms, I still care about the people behind it.
I value speed and momentum over precision in the early stages of any effort.
I am inclined to keep options open until the group has weighed in.
I value predictability in my daily routine because it lets me focus on what matters.
Most of the time, other people's suffering feels important to me.
Even when I am convinced that someone is being harmed, I feel little wish to see it stop.
When people are suffering, I want things to get better for them, whether or not I know them.
I instinctively create a chain of command when I work with others.
I would relocate to be closer to someone who needs my daily support.
I tend to receive compliments and praise with a sense of quiet satisfaction rather than elation.
I tend to direct the flow of conversation toward outcomes I envision.
I do not pick up on when someone is testing my reaction before committing to a stance.
I use tools like spreadsheets, project boards, or apps to keep my life organized.
I often do not realize that a conversation had multiple layers until someone explains it to me afterward.
When I feel rejected, the pain is immediate, physical, and consuming.
I notice the social signals that indicate someone is ready to end a conversation.
I routinely update my personal goals and adjust my life to match them.
I feel most at peace when I know I have put others before myself.
I speak in a way that signals the discussion remains open for others to shape.
I'd rather try something immediately and learn from the result than spend time planning it out.
I notice that witnessing an argument between other people activates my own nervous system as if I'm involved.
I plan my week on Sunday evening so Monday morning starts with clarity.
I would rather go without something I want so that someone else can have what they need.
